stories.title: Deutsche Bank Lends $85M for Miami Beach Condo Tower
stories.excerpt: Northlink Capital has secured $85 million of construction financing to develop a Miami Beach luxury condominium project, Commercial Observer has learned. Deutsche Bank provided the loan, which will refinance past debt and fund ground-up construction of the 12-story condo tower at 7200 Collins Avenue in Miami Beach’s North Beach neighborhood. Arrow Real Estate Advisors arranged the transaction with a team consisting of Morris Betesh, Alex Bailkin and Matt O’Hanlon. “7200 Collins brings efficiently designed, accessibly priced residences to one of North Beach’s premier oceanfront locations,” Betesh, managing partner at Arrow Real Estate Advisors, said in a statement. “With 96 percent of units under contract at closing, the project reflects strong buyer demand.” The 274,150-square-foot condo towers will comprise 222 units ranging from studios to two-bedrooms. Resident amenities will include a beach club, a swimming pool, a fitness center and rooftop sundecks along with ground-floor retail. Northlink Capital and Deutsche Bank did not immediately return requests for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Deutsche Bank finances $85M condo tower; 222 units, Miami Beach North Beach, 96% pre-sold.
Luxury residential project, 274K sq ft, efficient design targets accessible price point.
Strong buyer demand evident; oceanfront location, North Beach submarket desirability.
stories.summary: Northlink Capital secured $85 million in construction financing from Deutsche Bank for 7200 Collins Avenue, a 222-unit luxury condo tower in Miami Beach's North Beach neighborhood. The project is 96 percent pre-sold at closing, with units ranging from studios to two-bedrooms. Strong pre-leasing signals robust luxury multifamily demand in this Miami Beach submarket despite broader market headwinds.
stories.impact: Pre-sales at 96% in a luxury condo project indicate sustained high-end residential demand in Miami Beach North Beach, validating the market's appetite for oceanfront product. For multifamily developers, this signals that primary-market, well-positioned coastal properties remain attractive; however, the condo structure (not BTR) and pre-sale velocity suggest limited direct lessons for rental product underwriting, though it confirms Miami's continued draw for wealth migration.

stories.title: Data Center Operator Pursuing $500M San Antonio-Area Facility
stories.excerpt: CyrusOne is pursuing the construction of a 460,000-square-foot data center in Medina County. The project is estimated to cost $500 million. The facility is at 3397 U.S. Highway 90 W., just west of San Antonio The project, identified as “SAT14A,” has an estimated completion date of June 2027. The data center operator purchased roughly 57 acres off Highway 90 approximately seven miles from downtown Castroville in January. CyrusOne operates data center campuses in San Antonio, Austin, Dallas-Fort Worth and Houston. In San Antonio, its footprint includes the SAT1, SAT2-SAT4 and SAT5-SAT6 campuses on the city’s West Side, according to the company’s website. The San Antonio Business Journal reports that industry experts say the area’s available land and access to power have made it increasingly attractive to data center developers. stories.summary: CyrusOne is developing SAT14A, a 460,000-square-foot data center in Medina County, Texas, with an estimated $500 million capital outlay and completion targeted for June 2027. The company already operates multiple campuses across San Antonio, Austin, Dallas-Fort Worth, and Houston. Industry experts cite available land and power infrastructure as key drivers of data center concentration in the San Antonio region.
stories.impact: Major data center investment signals infrastructure readiness and employer attraction in the San Antonio metro; this typically precedes white-collar job growth and population in-migration. Multifamily developers should monitor San Antonio submarkets near Highway 90 and the tech/data corridor for downstream demand acceleration—corporate relocation and mid-market talent hiring often lag data center construction by 12–24 months, creating a window to acquire land and underwrite product ahead of rent growth.

stories.title: Phoenix BTR Investor Inks $73.1M Bridge Loan
stories.excerpt: Golden Horizons Enterprises inked a $73.1 bridge loan on Merrick on Camelback, a 334-unit built-to-rent community in Phoenix, Arizona. The financing was arranged by Lument and originated by Arcus Real Estate Capital. The bridge loan has a three-year term with two one-year extension options. Golden Horizon Enterprises recently paid $112.5 million for what was then called Bungalows on Camelback (Co-Star). It has since changed the name to Merrick on Camelback. Arcus Harbor maintains an exclusive correspondent relationship with Lument, referring all Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and FHA loans it originates to Lument for underwriting, processing, and closing. Arcus clients also have access to Lument’s balance sheet lending and other non-agency financing solutions. Merrick on Camelback is a gated build-to rent community with one-, two-, and three-bedroom floor plans in single-level living and private detached units. stories.impact: Bridge financing on a recently acquired Phoenix BTR asset indicates lender confidence in the submarket's fundamentals and the sponsor's repositioning thesis, but also signals near-term execution risk if markets soften. For multifamily developers in Phoenix, this reflects ongoing investor appetite for mid-market BTR, but watch cap rate compression and refinance readiness; if bridge rates remain elevated through 2027–2028, projects dependent on rapid stabilization may face margin pressure.

stories.title: Sales of U.S. Healthcare Real Estate Rise 77% Year-Over-Year
stories.excerpt: Sales of U.S. healthcare real estate rose 77% on a trailing 12-month basis in the second quarter of 2026, Avison Young reported. Meanwhile, net absorption reached 3.5 million square feet, continuing to exceed new deliveries, and occupancy rose to 92.4% while available space declined 4% year-over-year. One metric that is down from a year ago is the development pipeline: off 10% from Q2 2025. “We’re seeing a market that is increasingly defined by quality and scarcity,” said Jay Johnson, managing principal and healthcare sector leader, Avison Young. “Demand for well-located medical outpatient buildings remains strong, but the shrinking development pipeline could further tighten conditions and support rent growth in the years ahead.” Avison Young’s Q2 U.S. Healthcare Market Report highlights Houston, Los Angeles, Dallas, Chicago and Washington, DC as the nation’s most active healthcare leasing markets, while Los Angeles led investment sales activity during Q2. Rent growth is becoming more balanced across the quality spectrum, suggesting that demand is broadening beyond only the highest-quality assets, the report states. Pictured: The Bedford Collection, an outpatient medical portfolio in Beverly Hills, acquired in April 2026 by Douglas Emmett. bullets: Healthcare real estate sales rose 77% YoY through Q2 2026; net absorption 3.5M sq ft.
Occupancy 92.4%, available space down 4% YoY; development pipeline off 10% vs Q2 2025.

stories.summary: U.S. healthcare real estate sales jumped 77% year-over-year in the trailing 12 months through Q2 2026, with net absorption reaching 3.5 million square feet and occupancy rising to 92.4%, according to Avison Young. However, the development pipeline contracted 10% from Q2 2025, and available space declined 4%, indicating a tightening market. Houston, Los Angeles, Dallas, Chicago, and Washington DC emerged as the nation's most active leasing markets.
stories.impact: Shrinking healthcare pipeline and strong absorption set the stage for sustained rent growth across major metros, particularly in top-five leasing markets (Houston, LA, Dallas, Chicago, DC). Multifamily developers should note that healthcare projects often anchor mixed-use or transit-oriented development; lack of new healthcare supply may benefit nearby residential projects by reducing competing office/medical demand for prime locations, though robust healthcare capital deployment signals broader metro health and could drive ancillary residential demand if job growth accelerates.

stories.title: Triten Completes 3-Property Houston Apartment Portfolio Purchase
stories.excerpt: Triten Real Estate Partners acquired 3 Corners West, a 283-unit apartment community in Houston’s Memorial/Spring Branch submarket. The acquisition completes Triten and Evergen Equity’s purchase of the three-property 3 Corners multifamily portfolio after the partnership acquired 3 Corners North and 3 Corners East in November 2025. Together, the portfolio spans 997 units across more than 35 acres along Kempwood Drive, giving the firm full ownership of one of the area’s largest multifamily communities. With the full portfolio under its ownership, Triten will implement a value-add strategy. The three projects were built between 1972 and 1982. Located at 10105 Kempwood Drive, the 3 Corners community features one-, two- and three-bedroom floor plans ranging from approximately 730 to 1,280 square feet. Amenities include multiple swimming pools, a fitness center, covered parking and landscaped courtyards. JLL represented the seller in the transaction, while Triten represented itself. Evergen Equity was Triten’s capital partner on the portfolio acquisition. stories.summary: Triten Real Estate Partners, with Evergen Equity as capital partner, completed acquisition of the three-property 3 Corners multifamily portfolio totaling 997 units across more than 35 acres in Houston's Memorial/Spring Branch submarket. The portfolio, built between 1972 and 1982, is now under unified ownership and will undergo a value-add repositioning strategy. Unit mix ranges from one to three bedrooms, approximately 730–1,280 square feet, with standard amenities.
stories.impact: Consolidation of three older assets into a single platform indicates investor confidence in the Memorial/Spring Branch submarket's fundamentals and value-add opportunity set. For multifamily developers, this reflects ongoing institutional capital appetite for stabilized, lower-basis vintage product in established Houston submarkets; competitive pressure for acquisition may be rising, but buildable land constraints in this area suggest limited new supply, which could support rent growth and justify continued investment in adaptive reuse and repositioning plays.

stories.title: AI Firm Corgi to Open 24/7 Cafe at 121 East 27th Street
stories.excerpt: Alert the Queen, here come the corgis! OK, not exactly. Corgi Cafe, a 24/7 coffee shop from Corgi, an artificial intelligence-powered insurance company — no, really — is getting ready to open its first location in New York City, Commercial Observer can first report. The tenant, which will operate a round-the-clock cafe selling coffee, drinks and snacks, took 1,223 square feet of retail space at the base of 121 East 27th Street in Manhattan’s NoMad neighborhood, according to broker Meridian Capital Group. Corgi Cafe will take over the spot from event space and cocktail venue J. Bespoke. The length of Corgi’s lease runs through 2034, and there is an option for a five-year renewal. The asking rent was not disclosed, but Meridian’s website notes a monthly rent of $14,925 for the space, which is about three blocks northeast of Madison Square Park. The average asking rent for retail space in the nearby Herald Square area was $394 per square foot during the second quarter of 2026, according to CBRE data. Meridian’s Max Freudenberger and Michael Escava brokered the deal. Corgi Cafe was represented by Andrew Taub and Grace Zimmer from Newmark. Newmark did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. “The momentum along East 27th Street has been remarkable over the past several years. We’re seeing an increasing number of quality restaurant concepts choose this corridor, creating a true neighborhood dining destination,” Freudenberger said in a statement. “Our priority was finding a structure that aligned both parties’ objectives. Corgi Cafe moved decisively, knew exactly what they wanted, and the lease assignment allowed the transaction to come together efficiently while bringing an exciting new operator to the neighborhood.” Corgi Cafe, which did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment, has other cafe locations in San Francisco and Atlanta. The space was previously occupied by event venue J. Bespoke.

Non-traditional retail tenants (tech companies, startups) leasing smaller ground-floor spaces in NoMad suggest demographic resilience and may support premium residential rents nearby, though this is a tertiary signal relative to job market health and population retention.

stories.title: The Developers Trying to Make New York’s 485-x Multifamily Incentive Work
stories.excerpt: It’s become fashionable in New York City commercial real estate to bash the state’s 485-x program, which provides tax incentives for new residential development in certain areas of the five boroughs in exchange for including affordable housing. The criticism revolves around 485-x’s higher construction wage requirements in much of Manhattan and large swaths of the outer boroughs for projects with more than 99 units. Hence, the number of 99-unit projects. There were at least 154 such permits between April 2024 — the month 485-x took effect — and April 2026, per the City Reporter. But only 1 percent of those projects were over 100 units, according to the City Reporter, which cited data from the New York City Department of Housing Preservation and Development. By comparison, more than half of the buildings under the old 421-a program were over 100 units in the years before that incentive expired in 2022, BK Real Estate Advisors Chairman and CEO Bob Knakal wrote in a February Commercial Observer op-ed. For some developers, though, especially those not among the city’s largest, the de facto magic number under 485-x works. Or at least they’re willing to try to make it work. Andrea Gjini, the founder of AG Holdings Group, is one such developer. He’s not going above the 99-unit mark, though he would if the arithmetic was favorable in the long run — but it isn’t, he told Commercial Observer. “I just did the filing in a project and I wanted to make 120 units, and I let 21 units go, because the math for the project was not making sense,” Gjini said in an interview in June. “Expenses are 25 to 30 percent higher, and when you see the refinances that are coming up, and when you see the interest that they keep going up and down, it feels very uncertain to take a shot and to go beyond that number.” Building more units can equate to greater delays on the regulatory side as well, with one three-month delay on a project at 19 East 198th Street resulting in Gjini making three $150,000 m
bullets: 485-x tax incentive program driving 99-unit cap; at least 154 permits April 2024–April 2026.
Only 1% of projects exceed 100 units under 485-x vs >50% under prior 421-a program.
Higher prevailing wage requirements in Manhattan, outer boroughs disincentivizing projects >99 units.
stories.summary: New York State's 485-x tax incentive program, which took effect in April 2024 and offers tax breaks for residential development with affordable housing, has created a de facto 99-unit cap due to higher prevailing wage requirements for projects exceeding 99 units in much of Manhattan and the outer boroughs. At least 154 permits for 99-unit projects were filed between April 2024 and April 2026, with only 1% exceeding 100 units, compared to over 50% under the prior 421-a program.
stories.impact: The 99-unit cap under 485-x is fragmenting New York's multifamily development pipeline into smaller, less efficiently scaled projects, raising per-unit construction costs and reducing density in opportunity areas. For developers, this shifts underwriting math—smaller projects may have lower absolute development risk but face worse unit economics; the prevailing wage structure effectively prices out mid-market sponsors and favors larger firms with capital scale, concentrating supply and limiting neighborhood-level product diversity.

stories.title: The Athlete-Developers: Coming to a Community Near You
stories.excerpt: The World Cup’s excitement may be over, but one of the most fascinating sports phenomena hasn’t been visible on fields or courts. A cadre of athletes has been channeling their professional star power to develop commercial real estate projects. And some of those ventures are happening in those athletes’ hometowns. Hence, an intriguing addition to the real estate deal-maker’s playground has been the rise of the athlete-developer. Athletes from the NBA, NFL and other leagues, both active and retired, are reinventing themselves. They are learning the fundamentals of commercial real estate. They are forming key relationships in the industry. Potentially, they constitute a catalyst for urban development — an assist as effective as a ball court pass from Jalen Brunson or A’ja Wilson. G. Lamont Blackstone. Courtesy: Project REAP To illustrate, former NFL player Ndamukong Suh — who grew up in Portland, Ore. — is developing a hotel and conference center in his hometown via his company HMS Development. And the former Chicago Bulls star Derrick Rose has announced his involvement in a $7 billion mixed-use project planned for Chicago’s Near West Side. Both Suh and Rose serve as examples of athletes who are coupling their financial capital with the acquisition of intellectual capital — i.e., the knowledge that enables them to be active partners in hometown development projects. Suh had previously graduated from college with a degree in construction engineering. Rose is taking real estate classes for a year to learn the commercial real estate business. But this phenomenon hasn’t gone completely unnoticed. Troy Vincent Sr., executive vice president of football operations for the National Football League, looks favorably on this intersection of professional sports and commercial real estate. bullets: Retired and active professional athletes entering commercial real estate development; Ndamukong Suh, Derrick Rose cited.
Athletes leveraging hometown market knowledge and personal capital to develop hotels, mixed-use projects.
Emerging trend of athlete-developers as alternative sponsor class in underserved or secondary markets.
stories.summary: A growing cadre of professional athletes—both active and retired from NBA, NFL, and other leagues—are pivoting to commercial real estate development, often targeting their hometowns. Examples include former NFL player Ndamukong Suh developing a hotel and conference center in Portland, Oregon, via HMS Development, and former Chicago Bulls star Derrick Rose announced involvement in local real estate ventures. Athletes are leveraging their star power, local market relationships, and capital to drive development.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact in this article, though athlete-developers may become viable sponsors in secondary and tertiary markets (Portland, Chicago neighborhoods) where celebrity brand equity and local ties can unlock development rights or community support. For multifamily developers competing in these markets, monitor athlete-backed projects as competitive entrants; they may have non-traditional capital sources and tolerance for longer hold periods, but often lack professional CRE operating infrastructure.

stories.title: Lenovo Spending $145M on Greensboro-Area Plant Expansion
stories.excerpt: Lenovo opened its new smart campus in Whitsett for everyone to see. The new campus is located near Lenovo’s fulfillment center. The multi-million dollar facility will be used to build servers and manufacture products for customers in North Carolina. The $145 million investment expands the Whitsett facility footprint to 890,000 square feet (twice its original size). Manufacturing operations are already underway at the expanded facility originally built in 2007, with more than 400 positions filled and hundreds of additional jobs expected as production continues to scale. The Triad Business Journal reports Lenovo received an incentive package from the Guilford County Board of Commissioners worth around $1.16 million. Called the North Carolina Smart Campus (NCSC), the NCSC is part of Lenovo’s global manufacturing network of more than 30 regional facilities strategically located close to customers across 11 markets, including Argentina, Brazil, China, Hungary, India, Indonesia, Japan, Mexico, Saudi Arabia, the United States, and Vietnam. Lenovo, is the world’s largest personal computer manufacturer. The post Lenovo Spending $145M on Greensboro-Area Plant Expansion appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Lenovo investing $145M to expand Whitsett plant to 890K sq ft; doubled original facility size.

Guilford County incentive package $1.16M; Whitsett near Lenovo fulfillment center, North Carolina Triad.
stories.summary: Lenovo is investing $145 million to expand its smart campus in Whitsett, North Carolina, doubling the facility footprint to 890,000 square feet. Manufacturing operations are already underway, with 400+ positions filled and hundreds more expected as production scales. The company received approximately $1.16 million in incentives from Guilford County, and the facility supports regional server build and product manufacturing.
stories.impact: Lenovo's major manufacturing expansion in the Greensboro/Triad region signals durable industrial-sector demand and blue-collar job creation; this typically generates downstream demand for workforce housing and rental apartments in secondary markets. Multifamily developers should monitor Greensboro, High Point, and Triad submarkets for 200–300-unit workforce housing opportunities; a $145M factory investment often correlates with 500–1000+ indirect jobs and population in-migration over 2–3 years, supporting mid-market multifamily rents and occupancy.

stories.title: Brookfield Properties Rebrands as BGRE
stories.excerpt: Brookfield Properties is now BGRE. The rebrand, announced Sunday, reflects the real estate arm’s growth as a global operator and developer. The overhaul is in title only, however, and carries no changes for business operations or personnel, according to the announcement. “The rebrand to BGRE enables the platform to define its market-facing approach and continue to build its reputation as a premier, global real estate operating platform,” the announcement said. BGRE’s parent company, Brookfield Corporation, traces its roots to 1899 in São Paulo, Brazil, where it began as the São Paulo Tramway, Light and Power Company. The company evolved and rebranded over the decades through a series of incorporations and mergers that brought operations to Canada, and, in 1996, to the U.S. Today, BGRE is the developer and operator of more than 330 million square feet of office, logistics, hospitality, retail and residential space around the world, including the Manhattan West commercial complex. The BGRE rebrand follows on the heels of two major moves by the Brookfield Corporation. In June, Brookfield offloaded the Australia-founded global construction company Multiplex for $650 million to Japan’s Obayashi. Just a few weeks later, in early July, it was reported that Brookfield was in talks to replace Hines in the $3.5 billion Hudson Square Properties joint venture with Trinity Church Wall Street and Norges Bank Investment Management. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Brookfield Properties rebranded to BGRE; no operational or personnel changes; title-only rebrand.
BGRE operates 330M+ sq ft globally; office, logistics, hospitality, retail, residential; founded 1899.
Rebrand reflects growth as global real estate operator and developer; Manhattan West anchor portfolio.
stories.summary: Brookfield Properties announced a rebrand to BGRE (Brookfield Global Real Estate), effective immediately, to reflect the company's growth as a global real estate operating platform. The rebrand is title-only with no changes to business operations or personnel. BGRE operates more than 330 million square feet globally across office, logistics, hospitality, retail, and residential, and traces its roots to 1899.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact; rebranding is a corporate positioning move that does not signal strategy shifts or market sentiment changes. For multifamily developers, BGRE's substantial residential and mixed-use portfolio (including Manhattan West) continues to represent a major institutional competitor; monitor their underwriting and deployment pace for signals on cap rate and market sentiment, but the rebrand itself carries no market signal.
